s05a.slug: THURSDAY · 5:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS — TWO TEXTS
body: The RAZR is still warm from Ohio when it goes off again in his hand, twice, close together.

body.text: three suitcases. a crisis. come watch me fail
412. The labeled bags have arrived. Come and witness.

body: Skye’s has three suitcases in it and no capitals: by her standards, a distress flare. Theo’s is punctuated like a telegram from a duke.

The sun is down in the tops of the eucalyptus, and the light comes long and orange across the steps and over the pie box on his knees, and the bikes in the rack lay their shadows halfway to the road. Kevin won’t bring his mother’s van round to the Anacapa lot till eight. That leaves the better part of three hours, a pie, and two people who have each, in their own way, asked him to come and look at luggage.

s06s.slug: THURSDAY · 5:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THREE SUITCASES
body: Tomás is grinding coffee again, at suppertime, for reasons of his own. It comes up through the floor of her room in long ratcheting bursts, stops, starts again, and behind the house the surf is breaking at the bottom of the bluff, and in the window over the bed the sun has just gone into the Pacific and left it red.

Three suitcases lie open: one on the mattress, one on the floor, one on the desk chair with its lid tipped back against the wall. The clothes rack in the corner is down to bare hangers at one end. On the dresser, propped against the jar of beach glass, her white iPhone lies face-up on speaker, and Corinne is coming out of it from a car somewhere in Los Angeles with every consonant filed to a point.
“The skin person called me,” Corinne says. “She wants to know if you went outside today.”
Skye is on her knees beside the suitcase on the floor, her hair still stiff from the Point and a line of dried salt along her jaw. “No,” she says.
“Because they were very specific. A girl who’s been *indoors*.”
“Mm.”

Behind the phone’s back, for Jack in the doorway, she becomes the girl. She shrinks from the desk lamp with a forearm over her eyes. She sags by stages down the side of the suitcase, a houseplant somebody forgot in a closet, and comes to rest face-down in a pile of sweaters with one hand still raised so Corinne will know she’s listening.

“Car meets you in Vancouver. The sign won’t have your name on it, it’ll have the character’s, so look for *Cassie*. Wardrobe at two. And Skye. It’s two weeks. You’re furniture with lines. Be furniture.”
“Kay.”
“Text me from the gate.”
“Bye, Corinne.” She reaches up behind her with one bare foot and ends the call with her big toe.
She lifts her face out of the sweaters. “Three suitcases. It’s a crisis. I told you.”
“You said you’d fail.”

“I’m failing. Look at me.” She points without getting up. “That one’s Cassie. Cassie has been indoors. Cassie owns four cardigans and a feeling about her father. That one’s me. And that one’s the rain, because I looked it up, and Vancouver in February is the inside of a cloud with a Starbucks in it.”

The one on the bed won’t shut. She gets up and sits on it, and it still won’t, so he sits on it with her, side by side on Cassie’s cardigans with their knees touching, and she bounces once, businesslike, and the latch catches.
“Teamwork.” She keeps her seat, leaning on him, her shoulder under his arm; her hair smells like the Point. “Get my passport. Drawer under the glass. I can’t get up. If I get up, Cassie gets out.”

The drawer sticks and comes. Under a snarl of chargers and a roll of film in its canister, the passport is there, navy blue, the eagle on the cover worn soft at the corners from being carried. He opens it.

The girl in the picture is sixteen. Her braces have just come off — he can tell from the way she holds her mouth, still guarding them — and her hair is dyed a flat drugstore brown for some part he’ll have to ask about. Beside her face the government has typed her name in its block letters, the way it would type anybody’s.
He reads it off the page. “Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle.”
On the suitcase she holds still. She has her hands in her lap, and she watches his mouth while he says it.
“It’s the only thing I own that calls me that,” she says.
He has known the name a week. It looks different with an eagle on it. He’s still looking when she holds out her hand.
“Give it here. The Department of State has been very formal with me for three years. I don’t want you getting ideas.” She sets it on the dresser beside the phone, lined up with the edge.

His flannel is over the back of the desk chair, where it has lived since January, the salsa still on the cuff. She shakes it out, folds it in a way it would hurt Theo to watch, and lays it on top in the suitcase on the floor.
“That’s mine,” Jack says.
“It’s coming. It has a part.”
“What part?”

“Small. Recurring. It doesn’t say anything. It just turns up in scenes, and everybody knows what it means.” She pats it down. “On your way out, don’t open the door at the end of the hall. My afternoon’s in there drying.”
“The Point?”
“The Point. The rocks. Some surfer.” She pats the flannel again. “Don’t open it.”

Out of the lid pocket of the suitcase on the chair she pulls a few stapled pages, folded the long way and gone furry along the fold, and holds them out. PORT ALDER, it says across the top, and under that, *“Pilot” — Scene 14 — EXT. THE PORCH — NIGHT.* The girl’s lines are gone over in yellow highlighter. The other part is pink.
“Read with me.”
“Who’s pink?”

“Wade. Her father. He’s been gone fifteen years, and tonight he comes up the porch steps with a duffel bag and no explanation, which is a very strong choice for a man on network television.” She stands up in the middle of the rug in her socks. “Just read it. Don’t act. I can’t stand it when people act at me in my bedroom.”
He reads it. “Hi, kid.”

It comes out like a man reading the back of a cereal box, and it doesn’t slow her down. She’s already gone. She stands with her arms folded across herself, nineteen and furious, on a porch in a town that doesn’t exist, and looks at the place where Wade would be, which is Jack.
“It’s Cassie,” she says. “It’s been Cassie for a while.”
He finds the next pink. “You got tall.”
“I got fifteen years. Tall came with them.”
“I wrote you.”
“Twice. I have them both. I know what they say better than you do.” She takes a step toward a screen door that isn’t there. “I heard the truck, you know. That morning. I thought you forgot your —”

The line quits on her halfway. In the same motion she drops straight down, sitting, into the open suitcase on the floor, knees up, his flannel under her, and pulls the lid down over herself to the chin, a girl being packed for shipment, and says from inside it, in Corinne’s filed consonants, “Be furniture.”
Jack stands in the middle of her room with Wade’s page in his hand. He saw where it quit. He keeps his thumb on the place.
Downstairs, the grinder starts up again.

response: He reads it again, slower. “Hi, kid.” He gives it the porch steps first, and the duffel, and fifteen years of working up to it in a truck, and says it the way Wade might if he weren’t sure he was allowed to.

She climbs out of the suitcase. She finds her mark on the rug and folds her arms and starts again from *It’s Cassie*, and when she comes to the truck she goes through it — “I thought you forgot your thermos. I went to the window. I waited up for a *thermos*, Wade” — and on to the bottom of the page, where the writers have Cassie shut the screen door on him. She shuts it, on nothing, quietly.
Afterward she doesn’t look at him. She goes to the dresser, puts the passport back in the drawer under the jar of glass, and slides it shut.
“Seven-fifty,” she says, with her hand still on the drawer. “Go put things in a van. Nine-thirty. Knock.”
“Hi, kid,” he says, in Glenwood Avenue — flat, from the chest, with a pause after it you could park the Silverado in. Wade adds, off the page: “Close your mouth. You’ll catch flies.”
The suitcase shakes. She laughs inside it until the lid slides off her shoulders and she has to grab both sides to stay in.
“Again,” she says. “Louder. At the floor. Tomás has to hear this.”
So he gets down on his knees on her rug and says it into the floorboards, and downstairs the grinder stops mid-bean and doesn’t start again.

Her phone lights up on the dresser: CORINNE. She answers it on speaker with one finger, without picking it up — “Mm-hm” — and steers him to the door with her free hand in the middle of his back. “Seven-fifty. Go put things in a van. Nine-thirty. Knock.”
Behind them on the dresser Corinne is still talking, filing the edges off the word *Burnaby*, to a girl who is laughing at something else.
“You went somewhere on that line,” he says.
She looks up at him over the lid. “Professional secret.”
She climbs out, kneels, and brings the lid down over his flannel, fast, and her own fingers are still on the rim when it lands. He sees her leave them there.

She swears at the suitcase — one low word, in a voice he has never heard her do — and shakes the hand out and puts a knuckle in her mouth, and he looks at the hand and not at her face, and she seems to want it that way.
“Seven-fifty,” she says, and runs the zipper around three sides, over the flannel, and pats the top. “Go put things in a van. Nine-thirty. Knock.”
